conceptPrimer.heading: The Sine & Its Four Numbers
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Every AC question starts from one sentence: $v = V_m \sin(\omega t)$ with $\omega = 2\pi f$ and $T = 1/f$. A pure sine then owns four characteristic numbers. RMS (root-mean-square): square, average, take the square root — $V_{\text{rms}} = V_m/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707\,V_m$; it is the DC equivalent for heating, it is what every AC meter reads, and '220 V mains' is already an RMS value (its peak is $220\sqrt{2} \approx 311\text{ V}$). Mean value: the full-cycle average of a sine is ZERO (equal positive and negative loops), so the quoted figure is the HALF-cycle average $\frac{2V_m}{\pi} \approx 0.637\,V_m$. Form factor $= \frac{\text{RMS}}{\text{average}} = 1.11$ and peak (crest) factor $= \frac{V_m}{V_{\text{rms}}} = 1.414$. Micro-check: a 100 W bulb on 220 V draws $I = 100/220 = 0.454\text{ A}$ (RMS) while its peak voltage is 311 V — two different 'voltages', one lamp.

conceptPrimer.heading: Pure R, L, C: One Resists, Two Oppose the Change
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A resistor fights current regardless of waveform — voltage and current stay IN PHASE and $P = I^2R$ always. An inductor opposes any CHANGE of current through its back-emf (Lenz's law), so in pure $L$ the current LAGS the voltage by $90^{\circ}$, the opposition is $X_L = \omega L$ which GROWS with frequency, and the average power over a cycle is zero — the energy borrowed while current builds is returned as it collapses. A capacitor opposes any CHANGE of voltage (the current must charge it first), so current LEADS by $90^{\circ}$, the opposition is $X_C = 1/(\omega C)$ which SHRINKS as frequency rises, and again no net power is consumed. Micro-check: $L = 25\text{ mH}$ at $50\text{ Hz}$ gives $X_L = 2\pi(50)(0.025) \approx 7.85\,\Omega$ and $I = 220/7.85 \approx 28\text{ A}$ — a pure inductor limits current like a resistor but bills nothing.

conceptPrimer.heading: Phasors & the Impedance Triangle
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Because $V_L$ and $V_C$ are out of phase with everything else, series voltages must never be added arithmetically — the NCERT's own example shows $V_R + V_C = 311\text{ V}$ across a 220 V source, resolved only by the Pythagorean sum. Phasors are rotating vectors whose projections give the instantaneous values; for steady-state AC they reduce the whole circuit to one right triangle: horizontal leg $R$, vertical leg $X_L - X_C$, hypotenuse $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$, and $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$. The SIGN of the net reactance decides the character: $X_L > X_C$ — net inductive, current lags; $X_C > X_L$ — net capacitive, current leads; $X_L = X_C$ — pure resistance, in phase. Micro-check: $R = 30\,\Omega$, $X_L = 40\,\Omega$ gives $Z = 50\,\Omega$ and $\cos\phi = 30/50 = 0.6$ — the 3-4-5 triangle in disguise.

conceptPrimer.heading: Series RLC Swept Across Frequency
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Sweep the frequency of a series RLC and watch two reactances race in opposite directions: at low frequency $X_C$ dominates (circuit capacitive, current leads), at high frequency $X_L$ dominates (inductive, current lags), and exactly one frequency $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$ makes them meet and cancel. There $Z$ collapses to its minimum $Z = R$ — never below $R$, at any frequency — so the current peaks to $V/R$ and the power factor reaches unity. Below resonance the capacitor rules; above it the inductor rules; the phase angle $\phi$ slides smoothly from negative (leading) through zero to positive (lagging). Micro-check: $L = 0.1\text{ H}$, $C = 10\,\mu\text{F}$ gives $\sqrt{LC} = 10^{-3}\text{ s}$, so $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 10^{-3}} \approx 159\text{ Hz}$ — a radio-tuner answer in one line.

conceptPrimer.heading: Resonance Magnification: Q & Bandwidth
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Resonance does two opposite things at once: it MINIMIZES impedance (series circuit) and MAXIMIZES the voltage across the reactive elements — at $f_0$, $V_L = V_C = QV_S$ where $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{\omega_0 C R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}$ (all three forms agree at $\omega_0$). High $Q$ means small $R$: a taller, narrower current peak — better selectivity, bigger magnified voltages (which is why $QV_S > V_S$ must be respected in component ratings). Bandwidth measures the peak's width between the half-power ($1/\sqrt{2}$) points: $\Delta\omega = R/L$ in rad/s, or $\Delta f = \frac{R}{2\pi L}$ in Hz, and $Q = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega} = \frac{f_0}{\Delta f}$ — selectivity and bandwidth are the same coin. Micro-check: $R = 10\,\Omega$, $L = 0.1\text{ H}$ resonating at $\omega_0 = 1000\text{ rad/s}$ gives $Q = 10$ and $\Delta\omega = 100\text{ rad/s}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Power, Power Factor & Wattless Current
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Only resistance burns power, so the average power is $P = VI\cos\phi = I^2R$ with RMS values throughout — the $\cos\phi$ (power factor) is the fraction of the apparent power $S = VI$ that does real work. The power triangle stacks them: real $P$ (watts), reactive $Q_{\text{r}} = VI\sin\phi$ (VAR, sloshing between source and reactance), apparent $S = VI$ (VA) as the hypotenuse. A pure inductor or capacitor draws 'wattless' current — $\cos\phi = 0$, current flows, energy returns, net power zero — which is why an ideal $L$ or $C$ can never be the load that heats anything. Low power factor is expensive: for the same $P$, the current grows as $1/\cos\phi$, and transmission losses grow as its square — hence capacitors are added across inductive loads to pull $\phi$ toward zero. Micro-check: $V = 230\text{ V}$, $I = 5\text{ A}$, $\cos\phi = 0.8$ gives $P = 920\text{ W}$ while $S = 1150\text{ VA}$ — the difference is reactive ballast. (Balanced 3-phase: $P = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L \cos\phi$.)

keyFormulas.label: Sine Wave & Angular Frequency
keyFormulas.use: Convert to angular form BEFORE computing any reactance.

keyFormulas.label: RMS Value (Sine)
keyFormulas.use: The heating-equivalent DC value; what AC meters read; mains 220 V is RMS.

keyFormulas.label: Half-Cycle Mean Value
keyFormulas.use: Full-cycle average is zero — the quoted mean is over half a cycle.

keyFormulas.label: Form & Peak (Crest) Factors
keyFormulas.use: Sine-wave shape numbers — quotable, one-mark answers.

keyFormulas.label: Inductive Reactance
keyFormulas.use: Grows with frequency; current LAGS voltage by $90^{\circ}$ in pure $L$.

keyFormulas.label: Capacitive Reactance
keyFormulas.use: Shrinks as frequency rises; current LEADS voltage by $90^{\circ}$ in pure $C$.

keyFormulas.label: Series RLC Impedance
keyFormulas.use: The impedance triangle hypotenuse; never below $R$.

keyFormulas.label: Phase Angle & Power Factor
keyFormulas.use: Sign of net reactance decides lag (positive) or lead (negative).

keyFormulas.label: Phasor Voltage Sum
keyFormulas.use: Series branch voltages add phasor-wise, never arithmetically.

keyFormulas.label: Quality Factor (Three Equal Forms)
keyFormulas.use: Sharpness of resonance; also $V_L = V_C = Q V_S$ at resonance.

keyFormulas.label: Bandwidth
keyFormulas.use: Half-power width; quote the unit deliberately — rad/s vs Hz.

keyFormulas.label: AC Real Power
keyFormulas.use: RMS values only; real power lives in the resistance alone.

keyFormulas.label: Power Triangle
keyFormulas.latex: $S = VI\;(\text{VA}), \quad Q_r = VI\sin\phi\;(\text{VAR}), \quad S^2 = P^2 + Q_r^2$
keyFormulas.use: Apparent, reactive and real power — the three sides of one triangle.

keyFormulas.label: Balanced 3-Phase Power
keyFormulas.use: Line quantities for balanced three-phase loads (star or delta).

keyDefinitions.definition: The DC value that would deliver the same average heating in a resistor over a cycle; for a sine, $V_m/\sqrt{2}$ — the value AC meters report.
The algebraic mean of the waveform over half a cycle for a sine ($2V_m/\pi$); over a full cycle a pure sine averages to zero.
Ratio of RMS to mean value ($1.11$ for a sine); a shape descriptor of the waveform.
Ratio of peak to RMS value ($\sqrt{2} = 1.414$ for a sine); measures how spiky the waveform is.
Frequency-dependent opposition offered by an inductor ($X_L = \omega L$) or capacitor ($X_C = 1/\omega C$); the net series reactance is $X_L - X_C$.
The total phasor opposition of a circuit, $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$; its angle is the phase difference between V and I.
The angle by which the current leads ($X_C$ dominant) or lags ($X_L$ dominant) the voltage; zero at resonance and in pure resistive circuits.
$\cos\phi = R/Z$ — the fraction of apparent power doing real work; unity in pure resistance, zero in pure $L$ or $C$.
Current through a pure inductor or capacitor: the circuit returns every joule it borrows, so average power is zero despite non-zero current.
Q measures resonance sharpness ($\omega_0 L/R$) and equals the voltage magnification $V_L/V_S$; bandwidth is the half-power width $R/L$ rad/s — $Q = \omega_0/\Delta\omega$.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The peak value of the 220 V AC mains supply is approximately:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Mains ratings are RMS: $V_m = \sqrt{2} \times 220 \approx 311\text{ V}$. Insulation must survive the peak, not the RMS.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The inductive reactance of a $0.5\text{ H}$ inductor at $50\text{ Hz}$ is approximately:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $X_L = 2\pi fL = 2\pi(50)(0.5) \approx 157\,\Omega$ — convert to angular form first, then multiply.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: In a purely capacitive AC circuit, the current:

options.latex: is in phase with the voltage

mcqSelfTest.explanation: The charging current must flow BEFORE the capacitor voltage builds — current leads by $90^{\circ}$ (ELI the ICE man: ICE = C, I leads E).

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: A series circuit has $R = 60\,\Omega$ and $X_L = 80\,\Omega$. Its impedance and power factor are:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: 3-4-5 triangle: $Z = \sqrt{60^2 + 80^2} = 100\,\Omega$; $\cos\phi = R/Z = 60/100 = 0.6$. (Impedance is phasor addition, never $60 + 80$.)

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The resonant frequency of a series circuit with $L = 0.5\text{ H}$ and $C = 8\,\mu\text{F}$ is approximately:
At series resonance, the power factor of the circuit is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $X_L = X_C$ cancels the reactance, so $Z = R$ and $\cos\phi = R/R = 1$ — the circuit behaves as pure resistance (also $P = V I$, maximum for the given V).

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: A series RLC circuit has $R = 5\,\Omega$, $L = 0.5\text{ H}$, $C = 2\,\mu\text{F}$. At resonance, $Q$ and the bandwidth ($\text{rad/s}$) are:
Current in which circuit element can be 'wattless'?

options.latex: No element — all AC current dissipates power

mcqSelfTest.explanation: In pure L or C, $\phi = \pm 90^{\circ}$ so $\cos\phi = 0$ and average power is zero — the element returns all borrowed energy each cycle.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The form factor of a sinusoidal waveform is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Form factor = RMS/average $= 0.707/0.637 \approx 1.11$. (1.414 is the peak factor; 0.707 and 0.637 are the raw RMS and mean ratios.)

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: An AC load draws $4\text{ A}$ (RMS) at $230\text{ V}$ with a phase angle of $60^{\circ}$. The average power consumed is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $P = VI\cos\phi = 230 \times 4 \times \cos 60^{\circ} = 920 \times 0.5 = 460\text{ W}$. Option A forgot the power factor ($S = 920\text{ VA}$ is apparent power).

memoryHooks: The four sine numbers: RMS $0.707\,V_m$, half-cycle mean $0.637\,V_m$, form factor $1.11$, peak factor $1.414$.
ELI the ICE man: in L (ELI) E leads I; in C (ICE) I leads E.
$X_L = \omega L$ climbs with frequency; $X_C = 1/\omega C$ dives — they cross at resonance.
Series resonance trio: $Z$ minimum $= R$, current maximum, power factor $= 1$.
At resonance the reactances magnify: $V_L = V_C = Q V_S$ — respect component ratings.
$\omega = 2\pi f$ — convert to angular form BEFORE any reactance.
Real power lives in $R$ only: $P = VI\cos\phi = I^2R$; pure L and C are wattless.
Power triangle: $S = VI$ (VA) hypotenuse, $P$ (W) horizontal, $Q_r$ (VAR) vertical.
High $Q$ = small $R$ = tall narrow peak = high selectivity = big bandwidth inverse.
Bandwidth units: $\Delta\omega = R/L$ rad/s vs $\Delta f = R/(2\pi L)$ Hz — never mix them.
$Z \geq R$ always: any series-RLC answer below $R$ is a red flag, not a result.
commonMistakes: Mixing peak and RMS: inserting $V_m$ or $i_m$ into $P = VI\cos\phi$ — power formulas accept RMS values only.
Adding $X_L$ and $X_C$ as if both were positive: the net reactance is $X_L - X_C$, and its SIGN decides lag vs lead.
Adding series branch voltages arithmetically ($V_R + V_C > V_S$ 'paradox') — phasor (Pythagorean) addition is mandatory.
Reporting 'average of AC is zero' and then refusing to compute the half-cycle mean when the question explicitly asks for the average value.
Treating an ideal inductor or capacitor as a power consumer — each returns every joule it borrows; only $R$ dissipates.
Quoting $Q = \omega_0L/R$ while dropping $R$ or mixing $L$ and $C$ inconsistently with the equal form $Q = 1/(\omega_0CR)$.
Slipping on unit prefixes: $\mu F = 10^{-6}$ F, $\text{mH} = 10^{-3}$ H — one slip scales $f_0$ or $X$ by thousands.
Mixing degrees and radians inside $\phi$ (e.g. feeding degrees into $\tan^{-1}$ outputs assumed in radians) — pick one convention per line.
Confusing series resonance (impedance minimum, acceptor) with parallel resonance (impedance maximum, rejector) — the flip that examiners love.
examChecklist: Open every AC question by fixing the vocabulary: $v = V_m\sin\omega t$, $\omega = 2\pi f$, $T = 1/f$.
Know which factor is which: form factor 1.11 (RMS/mean), peak factor 1.414 (peak/RMS).
For any series RLC, sketch the impedance triangle ($R$, $X_L - X_C$, $Z$) before computing $\phi$ or the power factor.
State the resonance set together: $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$, $Z_{\min} = R$, $Q = \omega_0L/R = 1/(\omega_0CR)$.
Check $V_L = V_C = QV_S$ claims against component ratings — magnified voltages are real.
Power questions: $P = VI\cos\phi$ with RMS magnitudes; $\phi$ is the angle between V and I phasors.
Quote bandwidth units deliberately: rad/s ($\Delta\omega = R/L$) or Hz ($\Delta f = R/2\pi L$).
Reject any series-RLC answer with $Z < R$ — outside resonance it is impossible.
Sanity-check prefix arithmetic ($\mu$F, mH) before trusting a resonant frequency.
For 3-phase power, name the system (balanced) before using $P = \sqrt{3}V_LI_L\cos\phi$.
If a question says 'meter reading', default to RMS unless it names a PMMC/moving-coil instrument (average/DC content).
